justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a relatively stable near-term outlook with a slight upward drift over time. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 45.8 is anchored heavily on the most recent observed value or market price, assuming that short-term momentum and mean-reversion forces roughly balance out over such a brief window. For the one-week estimate of 46.0, I incorporated a modest positive drift, reflecting either a slight bullish bias in recent trend data or a small expected return assumption. By the one-month horizon, the estimate nudges up further to 46.5, continuing that gentle drift while acknowledging that over longer periods, any underlying fundamental or trend signal has more time to manifest. In all three cases, the point estimates are close together, suggesting the series is not expected to move dramatically in any direction over the near term.

The confidence interval widths grow substantially as the horizon extends, which reflects the natural accumulation of uncertainty over time. At one day, the 90% interval spans only 2.6 units (44.5 to 47.1), consistent with the relatively predictable short-term behavior of most financial or economic series where daily volatility is bounded. Over one week, the interval widens to 5 units, capturing the compounding effect of daily fluctuations and increased sensitivity to new information arriving throughout the week. By one month, the interval expands to 10 units (41.5 to 51.5), reflecting the much broader range of outcomes that become plausible when news events, policy changes, or macro shifts have time to accumulate and interact.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside these stated intervals. On the upside, a surprise positive catalyst — such as stronger-than-expected economic data, a policy announcement, or a sentiment shift — could drive values well above 51.5 at the monthly horizon. On the downside, adverse macro developments, geopolitical shocks, or a liquidity event could push values below 41.5. Even at the one-day horizon, the narrow interval assumes no major scheduled announcements or surprise news; an unexpected release could easily break through the 44.5–47.1 band.

It is also worth noting that my confidence intervals assume relatively stable volatility conditions. If realized volatility spikes — as it can during periods of market stress or policy uncertainty — then even the one-week interval could prove too narrow. Conversely, if conditions are unusually calm and the series is mean-reverting strongly, the one-month interval might prove wider than necessary. These intervals should therefore be treated as reasonable central estimates of uncertainty rather than hard bounds, and they carry their own model uncertainty on top of the underlying series uncertainty.
